1:
Delitzsch places the psalm by its neighbours: the earlier pair ran let Israel say and then peace be upon Israel; here the order reverses. He hears a deliverance already experienced, looked back on gratefully. What Israel confesses is that however sorely it was oppressed it has not succumbed. Clarke dates the writing after the captivity, the author unknown. Calvin narrows further: it was written when the church stood on the verge of destruction, his guess being the years after the return, when the Jews had almost fainted under Antiochus.

Calvin states the purpose as doctrine. God subjects his church to troubles so that he may better prove himself her deliverer; we despair because when our enemies are given loose reins our thoughts are engrossed with the evils harassing us, forgetting that the fathers' patience was tried the same way. He adds that the enemies are named by a bare pronoun, which aggravates the evil; Spurgeon reaches the same observation independently and gives a reason: Israel says they because it would be impossible to know all their names. Persecution, he concludes, is the heirloom of the church and the ensign of the elect.

Henry has the church speak as one person, old and grey-headed, recalling former days — a people oppressed beyond any other, a speckled bird all the birds peck at. They brought their troubles on themselves by their sins, he grants, but their neighbours hated them for the peculiarity of their covenant. Augustine traces the voice further back. The church is of ancient birth: once it was in Abel only, fought against by his lost brother, once in Enoch alone. Like Zacchaeus, little of stature but mighty in works, the psalm is short in words and large in sentiment. Ellicott adds that the youth is the nation's, the original having no adverb of time.

Verse 3 is where the best work is done. Henry notices the metaphors have been crossed: elsewhere it is the rod of the wicked upon the lot of the righteous, where one expects the plough, and here the plough upon the back, where one expects the rod. The enemies tore them as a husbandman tears ground with the share, wearing out the saints as long-tilled ground is worn out of heart; and God permitted it so that the fallow ground being broken he might sow the seeds of his grace, howbeit the enemies meant not so. Clarke sees a yoke instead, as though the people had been harnessed to the plough, which is how Jerome took it. Delitzsch corrects the word for furrow: it is not the furrow but the strip a ploughman takes at one time, at each end of which the team halts, turns and begins again. Ellicott reaches the same result from Wettstein, and calls the double image — the lash across a slave's back, the imprints of oppression left on the country as on the race — as striking as poetry ever produced.

Then they divide over whose back it is. Gill hears the Messiah, who gave his back to the smiters, and the Israelites scourged under the Maccabees, and reports the tradition that a Roman general ploughed up Jerusalem. Clarke will not have it. The words have been applied to the sufferings of Christ, he says, but he does not know on what authority: no such scourging could have taken place in his case, since it is not likely he received more than thirty-nine stripes, and the line about his whole body being one wound is unwarranted. Ellicott finds the bare statement that the Lord is righteous, dropped in without a conjunction, a revelation of how deep Israel's religion ran, and reads the cord as a slave's, cut so he goes free. Wesley glosses the cords as the enemies' plots and righteous as merciful — a sense Gill finds in the Hebrew too, where acts of mercy are called righteousness.
5:
The psalm turns to imprecation, and Henry hears it end as Deborah's song ended — so let all thine enemies perish, O Lord. He does not take the wish for a wish only: let them all be confounded is as much as to say they shall all be confounded. While God's people flourish as the loaded palm or the green and fruitful olive, their enemies wither as grass on a house-top, which is little, and short, and sour, and good for nothing. It perishes quickly, having no root; and the higher its position, which is perhaps its pride, the more it is exposed to the sun. He adds the sharpest observation here: the church's enemies wither of themselves, and do not wait to be rooted out by the judgments of God.

Gill and Clarke supply the natural history. Roofs in Judea were flat and covered with a plaster of terrace, so grass came up on them, small and weak, and burnt off by the summer sun. Clarke adds that the seeds arrive by accident and vegetate imperfectly for want of nourishment: if grass, the mower can make no hay of it; if corn, the reaper no sheaf. Let the Babylonians be like such herbage. Gill collects two travellers' reports. Menochius saw the same flat earthen roofs in Corsica, grass growing of its own accord and withering in summer; Olaus Magnus reports what Gill calls somewhat extraordinary — in the northern Gothic countries cattle are fed on the housetops, especially in a siege, the roofs turfed and sown with barley or oats so that they look like green meadows, and watered so diligently that what grows does not wither before it is plucked.

That last phrase is the disputed one, and Ellicott gives both sides. The clause has an Aramaic colouring and probably contains a textual error; the context seems to want before it is plucked up, a sense many scholars extract from a verb used elsewhere of drawing a sword or plucking off a shoe, read impersonally — which withereth before one pulls it up — favoured by the Greek, the Vulgate and Theodotion. But grass withering before maturity, growing as it does without soil like the seed on the rock in the parable, is exactly what one expects here, and suggests a more sudden destruction, the enemies perishing before their abortive plans can be carried out. So Ellicott keeps the received rendering, which Aquila, Symmachus and some Greek readings support. Clarke takes another route to the same place, glossing the verb as before it is unsheathed, before it ears. Wesley states it flatly: having no deep root it never comes to maturity, and all their designs shall be abortive.

Gill measures the failure by the harvest: such grass never rises high enough to be mowed, nor is there ever enough to fill a mower's hand.

The last verse turns on a custom all four describe alike. Passers-by greeted reapers at work and the reapers answered; Clarke and Gill cite Boaz coming to his field with the Lord be with you and receiving the Lord bless thee, and Ellicott says the closing line should be printed as the reapers' reply. Clarke draws the consequence historically: let their land become desolate, so no harvest appears in it again — which he says has literally happened, Babylon being destroyed and no harvests growing near where it stood. Henry draws it morally. Praying for harvest labourers is an ancient and laudable custom, but sacred expressions must never be used in light and ludicrous actions, and mowing grass off a house-top would be a jest; those who reverence God's name will not prostitute a salutation to it, since holy things must not be jested with. And it is dangerous to wish the church's enemies well in what they attempt, since whoever bids them God speed is partaker of their evil deeds.
